name: Ambika
summary: Ambika, or Kushmandini, is the Jain attendant goddess of the 22nd Tirthankara, Neminatha. She rides a lion, holds mangoes and is shown with her two sons.
about: Ambika is the yakshi, or attendant goddess, of Neminatha, the 22nd Tirthankara. Shvetambaras call her Ambika, meaning roughly 'Little Mother', while Digambaras call her Kushmandini. Jain texts say that she was once a woman named Agnila in Girinagar who was driven from home after giving food to a Jain monk, and who was reborn as a protector goddess; versions differ on the details. She is shown golden-coloured, riding a lion, holding a mango and children. She is linked to childbirth, family and wishes coming true. Jains of both main sects honour her, especially at Girnar in Gujarat and Shravanabelagola in Karnataka.
kidSummary: Ambika is a kind mother goddess in Jain stories. She rides a lion, holds mangoes and has two little sons beside her. Jains remember her as the protector of the Tirthankara Neminatha and pray to her for families and wishes.

story.title: A mother who gave food
story.text: Jain tradition says a woman named Agnila fed a Jain monk who was ending a long fast. In the story, her husband and the guests at the family ritual were angry because of it.

story.title: Sent away with her sons
story.text: Her husband sent her away with her two little sons. She sat under a tree on a hill and prayed.

story.title: Wonders in the forest
story.text: The story says a dry tree there grew fruit and a dry water tank filled up. Her husband, sorry, came to ask forgiveness.

story.title: A new birth
story.text: Frightened, Agnila leapt away from her husband (versions say from a cliff or into a well), and Jains say she was at once reborn as the goddess Ambika. Her husband, the story says, became the lion she rides.

story.title: A guardian of Neminatha
story.text: She became Neminatha's yakshi, a guardian of his teaching. In the Wikipedia retelling, her two sons later joined Neminatha's order. Jains still honour her with mangoes.

teaches: Kindness to those who are fasting or in need

family.name: Siddha and Buddha, or Shubhankara and Prabhankara

facts.text: Her name Ambika means roughly 'Mummy' or 'Little Mother'. Digambaras call her Kushmandini, after the kushmanda, a kind of pumpkin or gourd.
In the Shvetambara story, her husband Soma was furious when Agnila fed Neminatha's chief disciple Varadatta, who had been fasting for a month, with food meant for a ritual.
In the story, a dried-up mango tree on the hill grew fruit and an empty lake filled with water.
Her husband is said to have been reborn as the lion that carries her.

A Digambara legend says the anointing of the giant Gommateshwara statue would not flow below its navel until an old woman appeared with milk in half a white gullikayi fruit shell. Jains see her as Ambika, honoured there as Gullikayi Ajji.
Unlike the liberated Tirthankaras, Jains see Ambika as a soul still in the cycle of rebirth. That is why she can take part in the world and help people.
Jainpedia notes that a 14th-century manual of Shvetambara lay conduct, the Acaradinakara, includes a prayer to Ambika in the birth ceremony, asking her to keep the newborn safe.
A statue of Ambika found at Karajagi village in Karnataka carries a two-line inscription naming the day it was set up. It works out to Thursday, 27 April 1251.
In the Wikipedia retelling of the legend, some demigods were so angry at Agnila's treatment that they planned to flood the whole city of Girinagar, sparing only her house.
Ambika figures were carved in the ninth-century Jain caves at Ellora, in caves 32 and 33, according to Jainpedia.
In the 13th century Vastupala, a minister of the Chalukya rulers, compiled a hymn to Ambika called the Ambika-stavana.
In South India her skin is often painted dark blue, although tradition describes her as golden.

Scholars guess that Ambika blends three older ideas: a lion-riding goddess like Durga, a goddess of mangoes and mango trees, and Kushmanda. Ambika is also a common epithet of the Hindu goddess Parvati.
Wikipedia, citing Umakant Shah, names an Akota bronze of Ambika dated 550-600 CE as the oldest known sculpture of her, which makes it about 1,400 years old.
Jainpedia describes Ambika and the yaksha Sarvanubhuti as the model for later yaksha and yakshi pairs. Their figures stand on either side of a temple entrance on Chandragiri hill at Shravanabelagola.
The two sons differ by tradition. Shvetambara sources name them Siddha and Buddha, while Digambara sources name them Shubhankara and Prabhankara.
According to Wikipedia, Neminatha later initiated Ambika's two sons as monks, and she became his yakshi.
An Ambika sculpture from Dhar in Madhya Pradesh, dated 1034 CE, is now in the British Museum in London.
Wikipedia says the Ambika Temple at Girnar dates to 784 CE and is considered one of the oldest temples dedicated to her.
At Vimal Vasahi, one of the Dilwara temples, Ambika is carved as Kalpalata, a creeper that grants wishes. The name Kamana Devi also points to her wish-giving role.
The Art Gallery of New South Wales in Australia holds an 11th-century stele showing Sarvanubhuti and Kushmandini with Tirthankara figures.

quiz.q: Which Tirthankara is Ambika the yakshi of?
quiz.why: Ambika is the guardian goddess of the 22nd Tirthankara, Neminatha.
Jain tradition says her husband was reborn as the lion that carries her.
Her images show a mango and a mango-tree branch.

quiz.q: At which holy site do Jains tell how she finished bathing a giant statue with a little milk?
quiz.why: At Shravanabelagola, a Digambara legend says an old woman with milk in a fruit shell, understood as her, completed the anointing of the Gommateshwara statue.
